title: Indo-Greek Kingdom
neutral_summary:
The Indo-Greek Kingdom, also known as the Yavana Kingdom, were Hellenistic-era Greek kingdoms in the northwestern part of the Indian subcontinent covering most of modern-day Pakistan, parts of northwestern India and some eastern parts of Afghanistan. 
The term "Indo-Greek Kingdom" loosely describes a number of various Hellenistic states, ruling from regional capitals like Taxila, Sagala, Pushkalavati, and Bagram. Other centers are only hinted at; e.g. Ptolemy's Geographia and the nomenclature of later kings suggest that Theophilus in the south of the Indo-Greek sphere of influence may also have had a royal seat there at one time. 
The kingdom was founded when the Graeco-Bactrian king Demetrius I of Bactria invaded India from Bactria in about 200 BC. The Greeks to the east of the Seleucid Empire were eventually divided to the Graeco-Bactrian Kingdom and the Indo-Greek Kingdoms in the North Western Indian Subcontinent.
During the two centuries of their rule, the Indo-Greek kings combined the Greek and Indian languages and symbols, as seen on their coins, and blended Greek and Indian ideas, as seen in the archaeological remains. The diffusion of Indo-Greek culture had consequences which are still felt today, particularly through the influence of Greco-Buddhist art. The ethnicity of the Indo-Greek may also have been hybrid to some degree. Euthydemus I was, according to Polybius, a Magnesian Greek. Euthydemus I was an Ionian-Greek from one of the Magnesias in Ionia, though it is uncertain from which one (Magnesia on the Maeander or Magnesia ad Sipylum). His son, Demetrius I, founder of the Indo-Greek kingdom, was therefore of Greek ethnicity at least by his father. A marriage treaty was arranged for the same Demetrius with a daughter of the Seleucid ruler Antiochus III. The ethnicity of later Indo-Greek rulers is sometimes less clear. For example, Artemidoros (80 BC) was supposed to have been of Indo-Scythian descent, although he is now seen as a regular Indo-Greek king. 
Menander I, being the most well known amongst the Indo-Greek kings, is often referred to simply as "Menander," despite the fact that there was indeed another Indo-Greek King known as Menander II. Menander I's capital was at Sakala in the Punjab (present-day Sialkot). Following the death of Menander,  most of his empire splintered and Indo-Greek influence was considerably reduced. Many new kingdoms and republics east of the Ravi River began to mint new coinage depicting military victories.  The most prominent entities to form were the Yaudheya Republic,  Arjunayanas, and the Audumbaras. The Yaudheyas and Arjunayanas both are said to have won "victory by the sword". The Datta dynasty and Mitra dynasty soon followed in Mathura.
The Indo-Greeks ultimately disappeared as a political entity around 10 AD following the invasions of the Indo-Scythians, although pockets of Greek populations probably remained for several centuries longer under the subsequent rule of the Indo-Parthians, the Kushans, and the Indo-Scythians, whose Western Satraps state lingered on encompassing local Greeks, up to 415 AD.

positions.A: The Indo-Greek rulers and their kingdom remained fundamentally Greek in ethnicity and identity, with figures like Demetrius I tracing clear Greek ancestry through Euthydemus I.
positions.B: The Indo-Greek rulers and their kingdom became substantially hybridized with local Indian and Central Asian populations, making later kings' Greek identity uncertain or largely nominal.

title: Early Kurdish nationalism
neutral_summary:
The nationalist movement ( also known as the Pan-Kurdism ) among the Kurdish people first emerged in the late 19th century with an uprising in 1880 led by Sheik Ubeydullah. Many Kurds worked with other opponents of the Ottoman regime within the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP). A growth in ethnic consciousness at the start of the 20th century was spearheaded by the Society for the Elevation of Kurdistan. Some Kurdish nationalist groups agitated for secession, others for autonomy.
During the First World War, while some Kurdish nationalists were working with the British and Russian enemy powers, Kurdish tribal forces were fighting alongside Ottoman troops on the Russian front. Deaths and displacements occurred on a large scale among Kurdish civilians due to wartime conditions and deliberate ethnic cleansing policies.
There was a brief opportunity for Kurdish nationalism after World War I with the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire.  Western powers (particularly the United Kingdom) promised the Kurds they would act as guarantors for Kurdish freedom, a promise they subsequently broke. Some of the autonomist Kurdish groups received British support leading up to the Treaty of Sèvres (1920), which prepared for local autonomy for the Kurdish regions and envisaged later independence. Opposition from Kemal Atatürk, leader of the new nation-state of Turkey, and changes in British policy, prevented such a result. Following the Treaty of Lausanne (1923) the Kurdish territory was partitioned between Turkey, the French mandate of Syria, the British mandate of Iraq, and Persia.

positions.A: Kurdish nationalism represented a legitimate self-determination movement betrayed by Western powers who reneged on promises of autonomy and independence after World War I.
positions.B: The post-Ottoman territorial settlement, which partitioned Kurdish-inhabited lands among Turkey, Syria, Iraq, and Persia, was a justified outcome of regional geopolitical realities rather than a betrayal of the Kurds.

title: Iraqi Turkmens
neutral_summary: The Iraqi Turkmens (Turkish: Irak Türkmenleri, عراق تورکمنلری; Arabic: تركمان العراق), also referred to as Iraqi Turks, (Turkish: Irak Türkleri, عراق توركلری; Arabic: أتراك العراق) are the third largest ethnic group in Iraq. Their traditional homeland is in northern Iraq, mainly Kirkuk and Nineveh provinces, with Kirkuk considered by them as their capital. They have close cultural ties with Turkey, and are closely related to Syrian Turkmen. Iraqi Turkmens in Iraq do not identify with the traditionally-nomadic Turkmens of Central Asia.

positions.A: Kirkuk and its surrounding areas constitute the historic homeland and rightful cultural capital of the Iraqi Turkmens, whose demographic and political weight there should be officially recognized.
positions.B: Kirkuk is a multi-ethnic Iraqi province whose status should not be defined around Turkmen claims, as competing Kurdish and Arab communities have equally valid historical and demographic claims to the region.

title: Sykes–Picot Agreement
neutral_summary:
The Sykes–Picot Agreement () was a 1916 secret treaty between the United Kingdom and France, with assent from Russia and Italy, to define their mutually agreed spheres of influence and control in an eventual partition of the Ottoman Empire.
The agreement was based on the premise that the Triple Entente would achieve success in defeating the Ottoman Empire during World War I and formed part of a series of secret agreements contemplating its partition. The primary negotiations leading to the agreement took place between 23 November 1915 and 3 January 1916, on which date the British and French diplomats, Mark Sykes and François Georges-Picot, initialled an agreed memorandum. The agreement was ratified by their respective governments on 9 and 16 May 1916.
The agreement effectively divided the Ottoman provinces outside the Arabian Peninsula into areas of British and French control and influence. The British- and French-controlled countries were divided by the Sykes–Picot line. The agreement allocated to the UK control of what is today southern Israel, Jordan and southern Iraq, and an additional small area that included the ports of Haifa and Acre to allow access to the Mediterranean. France was to control southeastern Turkey, the Kurdistan Region, Syria and Lebanon.
As a result of the included Sazonov–Paléologue Agreement, Russia was to get Western Armenia in addition to Constantinople and the Turkish Straits already promised under the 1915 Constantinople Agreement. Italy assented to the agreement in 1917 via the Agreement of Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne and received southern Anatolia. The Palestine region, with a smaller area than the later Mandatory Palestine, was to fall under an "international administration".
The agreement was initially used directly as the basis for the 1918 Anglo–French Modus Vivendi, which provided a framework for the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration in the Levant. More broadly it was to lead, indirectly, to the subsequent partitioning of the Ottoman Empire following Ottoman defeat in 1918. Shortly after the war, the French ceded Palestine and Mosul to the British. Mandates in the Levant and Mesopotamia were assigned at the April 1920 San Remo conference following the Sykes–Picot framework; the British Mandate for Palestine ran until 1948, the British Mandate for Mesopotamia was to be replaced by a similar treaty with Mandatory Iraq, and the French Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon lasted until 1946. The Anatolian parts of the agreement were assigned by the August 1920 Treaty of Sèvres; however, these ambitions were thwarted by the 1919–23 Turkish War of Independence and the subsequent Treaty of Lausanne.
The agreement is seen by many as a turning point in Western and Arab relations. Arabs saw it as the failure to keep a British promise in the McMahon–Hussein correspondence with Hussein bin Ali, King of Hejaz regarding a national Arab homeland in exchange for supporting the British against the Ottoman Empire. The British later claimed that Palestine was meant to be excluded from the area of Arab rule, as it is technically located west of Damascus: for obvious reasons the Zionists took the same position. The Arabs interpreted the letter as it reads: Lebanon, not Palestine, is to the west of Damascus and the other areas mentioned. The agreement, along with others, was made public by the Bolsheviks in Moscow on 23 November 1917 and repeated in The Manchester Guardian on 26 November 1917, such that "the British were embarrassed, the Arabs dismayed and the Turks delighted". The agreement's legacy has led to much resentment in the region, among Arabs in particular but also among Kurds who were denied an independent state.

positions.A: The Sykes–Picot Agreement was a legitimate wartime diplomatic arrangement between allied powers that provided a necessary framework for administering former Ottoman territories after the empire's defeat.
positions.B: The Sykes–Picot Agreement was a colonial betrayal that arbitrarily carved up Arab lands for European imperial interests, contradicting earlier promises of Arab independence and creating lasting regional instability.

There is ongoing debate regarding whether he followed National Socialist ideology or whether collaboration with the Nazi regime was purely opportunistic in the pursuit of Kurdish independence. title: Uri Tzafon
neutral_summary: Uri Tzafon (English: "Awake, O North") is a far-right grassroots movement based in Israel that promotes a permanent revision of the northern border of Israel with neighbouring Lebanon. The movement started in 2024 as a niche initiative promoting the annexation of the territories south of the Litani River, before growing significantly in popularity following the 2026 Iran War and the 2026 Lebanon War. Whilst the main goal remains to settle the territories of the Litani River and "Judaize them", the movement's expansionist goals have recently also started to include all the territories south of the Zahrani River. As of 2026, the movement has become mainstream; however, it continues to face backlash by some analysts and members have been arrested over the years due to illegal crossings into Lebanon.

title: Deswali Majhi
neutral_summary:
Deswali Majhi is a Hinduized section of Santal tribe, distributed in western region of West Bengal and eastern region of Jharkhand in India. The community took shape after the great Santal rebellion (1855–56) by adoption of Hinduism due to oppression faced as a Santal by the Britishers and their proximity to the Bengali people.

Tribals known as Deswali Manjhis are those Santhals who, before the current tendency among Santhals to regard themselves as Hindus, came within the Hindu fold. According to H. H. Risley, “Deswali Manjhis are a subtribe of Santhals in the south of Manbhoom, who employ Brahmans (for officiating in religious observances) and have adopted portions of Hindu rituals”.

positions.A: The adoption of Hinduism by Deswali Majhi Santals represents a loss of authentic tribal identity driven by colonial-era oppression and social pressure to assimilate into the Bengali Hindu mainstream.
positions.B: The adoption of Hinduism by Deswali Majhi Santals represents a legitimate cultural and religious evolution that allowed the community social mobility and integration without erasing their Santal heritage.

title: Kundwana
neutral_summary: Kanduana, (Urdu: کندوآنہ); Kundwana, Kunduana, or Kundoana is a clan of the Punjabi Gujjars found in Pakistan and India.

positions.A: Kundwana (Kanduana) is a distinct and historically legitimate clan within the Punjabi Gujjar community of Pakistan and India.
positions.B: Kundwana is not a clearly distinct clan but rather a loosely defined or disputed sub-group label within the broader Gujjar community.

title: Sevayat
neutral_summary:
Sevayat (pl. sevāyatas; Sanskrit: सेवायत, romanized: sevāyat; Odia: ସେବାୟତ, romanized: sebāyata, lit. 'One who performs service') is a term for a group of hereditary temple servants who work at the Jagannath Temple in Puri and do ritual, administrative, and service work in a structured caste system. The Sevayat community is made up of many different caste groups, such as Brahmins, non-Brahmin service castes, and tribal groups like the Daitas. Each group has its own hereditary roles based on long-standing temple traditions. Their jobs include priestly worship and preparing offerings, as well as managing the logistics of rituals and festivals. They are an important part of the temple's daily operations and annual events like the Ratha Yatra. 
The Sevayat system is an example of a ritual-occupational hierarchy in Hindu temple institutions. It is based on customary laws and written records like the temple's Record of Rights. The system combines religious duty with social identity and hereditary privilege. Sevayats traditionally use specific ritual colours in their attire and temple practice.

positions.A: The hereditary, caste-based Sevayat system preserves essential temple traditions and ritual expertise that should be maintained as customary law dictates.
positions.B: The hereditary, caste-based Sevayat system perpetuates social inequality and exclusion and should be reformed to allow broader, merit-based participation.

title: Vadrangi
neutral_summary: Vadrangi is a community in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana Kerala in India. They were part of Vishwabrahmin group. Their traditional profession is carpentry. They are classified as part of the Other Backward Class category according to Reservation in the government.

positions.A: The Vadrangi community's traditional caste-based occupation of carpentry justifies their continued classification under the Other Backward Class category for reservation benefits.
positions.B: Caste-based reservation classifications like that applied to the Vadrangi community are an outdated approach that should be reassessed rather than tied to traditional occupational identity.

title: Kanchari
neutral_summary:
Kanchari is a community in Andhra Pradesh, India also known as Kanchara, Kanchera and Musarlu.
The community's name is derived from kanchu (bronze) and their traditional profession was bronze-making. They are part of Vishwakarma group. They are classified as a Backward Class in India's system of positive discrimination.

positions.A: The Kanchari community's classification as a Backward Class is justified given their historical socio-economic marginalization and traditional occupational status as bronze-workers.
positions.B: The Kanchari community's continued classification as a Backward Class is an outdated categorization that should be reassessed given changing socio-economic conditions.

title: Hakla
neutral_summary: Hakla, sometime spelled as Haklla or Akla, is a clan originally affiliated with the Gurjar/Gujjar ethnic group of South Asia. They are mostly found among the Hindu and Muslim Gujjars.

positions.A: Hakla is a distinct clan whose origins and identity are legitimately tied to the Gurjar/Gujjar ethnic group of South Asia.
positions.B: Hakla's classification as a Gurjar/Gujjar sub-clan is disputed or overstated, and its ethnic affiliation is not clearly established.

title: Adi Andhra
neutral_summary:
Adi-Andhra is a Telugu caste found in the Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, primarily in the Coastal Andhra region. They are categorised as a Scheduled Caste by the Government of India.
Adi-Andhra literally means 'the original people of Andhra'. The Adi-Andhra group is a composite caste that consists of about 60% of Malas and 40% of Madigas, who belong to the second and third generation of educated scheduled castes. Many Adi-Andhras are engaged in modern occupations created by western education. A small section of Adi-Andhra also lives in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
As per the 2001 census, Adi-Andhra constituted 9% of the total Scheduled Caste (SC) population of United Andhra Pradesh. As per the 1981 census, Adi-Andhras had the highest literacy rate among the Dalit castes of Andhra Pradesh. They are the most advanced group in terms of education and employment among the SCs in Andhra Pradesh.

positions.A: Adi-Andhra should be recognized as a legitimate, distinct composite caste identity that unites the more educationally and economically advanced sections of Malas and Madigas.
positions.B: Adi-Andhra is not a genuinely separate caste but a label adopted by already-advantaged sections of Malas and Madigas, and its inclusion in the general SC category unfairly diverts reservation benefits from less advanced Dalit subgroups.

title: Chopra clan
neutral_summary:
Chopra, is a clan found in the Gurjar Punjabi ethnic community of Pakistan and India.
They are mainly adherents of Hinduism, Sikhism and Islam. The variations of the name include Chopra, Chonpra, or Chupra.

positions.A: The Chopra clan's origins and status are rooted in Gurjar ancestry, linking them to the broader Gurjar Punjabi ethnic community.
positions.B: The Chopra clan's claimed Gurjar ancestry is a constructed or contested identity rather than a historically verified lineage.

title: Arain (Delhi)
neutral_summary: The Arain of Delhi are an Urdu-speaking Muslim community found in Delhi, India.

positions.A: The Arain of Delhi are descended from Rajput or Arab ancestors, reflecting a noble or foreign lineage.
positions.B: The Arain of Delhi are an indigenous agrarian caste whose identity stems from their historical occupation as cultivators rather than any noble or foreign descent.

title: List of Scheduled Castes in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana
neutral_summary:
The Dalits, once referred to as "untouchables" and currently recognized as Scheduled Castes by official designation, make up around one-sixth of India's population. These Scheduled Castes are predominantly concentrated in rural areas. Throughout centuries, they have endured the status of second-class citizens and were often excluded from India's varna system, a social hierarchy.
As per the 2011 census of India, in the United State of Andhra Pradesh, the total population of Scheduled Castes is 13,878,078 individuals, comprising 6,913,047 males and 6,965,031 females. Out of this population, 10,846,333 people live in rural areas. This represents approximately 6.89% of India's total Scheduled Caste population, which stands at 201,378,086.
Andhra Pradesh, prior to the formation of Telangana, comprised 60 distinct castes. Following the creation of Telangana, the Beda (Budga) Jangam caste was excluded from the list of Andhra Pradesh, while the Godagali caste was removed from Telangana. Consequently, each state now consists of 59 castes, reshaping the demographic composition in the aftermath of the state division.

positions.A: The reclassification of Scheduled Castes after Telangana's formation (excluding Beda Jangam from Andhra Pradesh and Godagali from Telangana) accurately reflects the distinct regional and social realities of each new state.
positions.B: The removal of communities like Beda Jangam and Godagali from the respective state SC lists unfairly strips deserving groups of constitutional protections and welfare benefits based on arbitrary administrative boundaries.

title: Sembadavar
neutral_summary: Sembadavar  or Parvatha Rajakulam is a traditional fisherman community found mainly on the Coromandel coast of the Indian state of Tamil Nadu and union territory of Pondicherry. They also take the title Nattar.  Sembadavar are a maritime community who are occupied primarily as inland and river fishermen and primarily fish with fishing nets. Some Sembadavars migrated to Andhra Pradesh and Telangana to form a caste called Sambuni Reddi. There are many theories as to their origins but they have since ancient times been recorded in the area of Tamil Nadu, Pondicherry and Sri Lanka.

positions.A: Sembadavar origins and status should be traced through theories linking them to broader Tamil fishing and maritime caste traditions with historical ties to Sri Lanka.
positions.B: Sembadavar should be recognized as a distinct caste group, the Parvatha Rajakulam/Nattar, with its own separate lineage independent of other fishing communities.

title: Harni
neutral_summary: The Harni are a Muslim community found in the province of Punjab, Pakistan. and also found in Punjab, India.

positions.A: The Harni are a distinct Muslim community with a unique historical and social identity deserving separate recognition.
positions.B: The Harni are not a genuinely distinct group but rather a subset of broader regional or caste identities in Punjab.

title: Nirdhi Bhil
neutral_summary:
Nirdhi Bhil or sometimes pronounced as Nilde Bhil are a Muslim community found in India.
Some Bhil, it is said to have occurred during the rule of the Faruki kings. Satmalas hills formed part of the territory the Faruqi kingdom, a medieval state in central India. A close association had developed between the Bhil of this region, and the Faruqi state led to the conversion of many of them to Islam.

positions.A: Nirdhi Bhil should be officially recognized as a Scheduled Tribe group entitled to tribal reservation benefits because of their direct descent from the Bhil tribal community.
positions.B: Nirdhi Bhil should not be classified under Scheduled Tribe status because their conversion to Islam under Faruqi rule makes them a distinct religious community rather than part of the traditional Bhil tribal fold.

title: Lali (tribe)
neutral_summary: The Lali, sometimes written as Lalee, are a Jat clan, found mainly in Chiniot District of Punjab, Pakistan. Wali Muhammad Lali from Lalian was the most powerful figure of history of Lali family.

positions.A: The Lali are a distinct Jat clan with a documented genealogical history centered on Wali Muhammad Lali and the Lalian region.
positions.B: Claims about the Lali clan's distinct identity and historical prominence are based on limited or unverifiable genealogical sources typical of caste/clan self-histories.

title: Tas (clan)
neutral_summary: Tas is an agricultural clan of the Indian and Pakistani Gurjar ethnic community in Indian Punjab. Tas Gujjars are adherents of Hinduism, Islam and some are also Sikh.

positions.A: Tas is a legitimate sub-clan of the Gurjar ethnic community with a distinct agricultural and historical identity in Punjab.
positions.B: The classification of Tas as a Gurjar clan is disputed and may reflect contested or unverified genealogical claims rather than established ethnographic fact.

title: Dhandla
neutral_summary:
Dhandla is a Punjabi Muslim clan and surname, originating from the Bhatti Rajputs.

Muhammad Zafar Ullah Khan Dhandla

title: Kardar (surname)
neutral_summary: Kardar is a surname and a Punjabi Arain clan of mainly Pakistan, Iran and Afghanistan.

positions.A: The Kardar clan should be classified primarily as an Arain sub-group rooted in Punjabi identity.
positions.B: The Kardar clan's identity extends beyond Punjabi Arain classification to broader regional communities in Pakistan, Iran, and Afghanistan.

title: Noon (surname)
neutral_summary:
Noon is a surname and Punjabi clan of India and Pakistan. They are categorized both Rajput and Jat. It can also be a variant of Noone, a surname of Gaelic origin.
Notable people with the surname, who may or may not be affiliated with the clan, are listed below.

positions.A: The Noon clan should be classified as Rajput, reflecting a lineage of martial and ruling status.
positions.B: The Noon clan should be classified as Jat, reflecting an agrarian tribal identity rather than Rajput status.

title: Dhamyal (caste)
neutral_summary: The Dhamyal (Also spelled Dhamial) is a tribe found in India and Pakistan and believed to derive its name from the  Rajput Janjua king, Dhami Khan Rajput.

positions.A: The Dhamyal tribe's name and lineage derive from Dhami Khan, a Rajput Janjua king, establishing a Rajput ancestral claim.
positions.B: The Dhamyal tribe's origin and naming are independent of any Rajput Janjua royal lineage and reflect a separate genealogical history.

title: Thikariya
neutral_summary: Thikariya or Thikriya is a subcaste of the Thakkar clan, found among the Muslim and Hindu and possibly some Sikh Gujjars. The variations of the clan name include Thikariya, Thikria, Thikaria, Thekaria, or Thekria.Renowned personalities amongst the Thikaria clan include Baba Jee Chaudhry Ilyas Khan Theekriya Gujjar and Advocate Aftab Ahmed Gujjar

positions.A: Thikariya is a legitimate subcaste of the Thakkar clan within the broader Gujjar community, spanning Muslim, Hindu, and Sikh members.
positions.B: The classification of Thikariya as a distinct subcaste of the Thakkar clan is disputed or lacks sufficient documented basis to be treated as an established caste category.

title: Dholi (caste)
neutral_summary:
Dholi is a traditional community of musicians, found primarily in Western India and used to play drums and Dholak in religious festivals. They are not a separate caste but a group of different communities engaged in the service of drumming and playing musical instruments in village festivals and related auspicions. They were considered as socially and economically backward residing in the rural areas.
Initially, they were not a specific caste but with the time the occupation of drum-playing became herediatery which lead to creation a Dholis as a caste, which was derived for the word 'Dhol' and includes member of other castes and tribes accumulated to form the group. Due to social backwardness and being in the lowest in the strata of caste system, they are recognized as Scheduled Castes.
In present times, they works as artisans and music professionals in functions and are considered as an important part of Culture of Rajasthan.

positions.A: Dholi should be classified and treated as a distinct hereditary caste, warranting its recognized Scheduled Caste status and associated protections.
positions.B: Dholi is not truly a separate caste but an occupational grouping of diverse communities and tribes, so its formal caste classification and Scheduled Caste status are a misclassification of a functional identity.

title: Malai Vellalar
neutral_summary:
Malai Vellalar is a Tamil-speaking community from South India, especially the state of Tamil Nadu.
They are Hindus and follow Phratry system. They mostly reside in hill regions and engage in various occupations such as agriculture and trade for their living.

positions.A: Malai Vellalar should be officially classified and recognized as a Scheduled Tribe given their historical residence in hill regions and distinct socio-cultural practices.
positions.B: Malai Vellalar should not be granted Scheduled Tribe status, as they are more accurately classified within existing Backward Class or other caste categories.

title: Korri
neutral_summary:
Korri is a clan of the Gurjar people of southern Asia.
They're irrespectively found among the Hindu and Muslim Gujjars. They principally live in the areas like Punjab, Pakistan, Azad Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and Jammu and Kashmir.

positions.A: The Korri are a distinct and legitimate clan within the broader Gurjar community, spanning both Hindu and Muslim adherents.
positions.B: The Korri are not a separate clan but rather a sub-group or offshoot of another established Gurjar clan, and their independent clan status is questionable.

title: Sayhul
neutral_summary: Sayhul (Urdu: سیہول), also spelled Sehul, Sehol or Sehole, is a Jat clan of Punjabis, found in Pakistan and India, mainly in Faisalabad, Sheikhupura, Gujranwala, Jhelum and other areas in central Punjab. Sayhul are said to be descended from Chauhans.

positions.A: Sayhul are a Jat clan descended from the Chauhans, as claimed by their own oral tradition and genealogical accounts.
positions.B: The claimed Chauhan descent of Sayhul is an unsubstantiated genealogical claim lacking independent historical verification.

title: Semwal
neutral_summary: Semwal is one of the thirty-six subcastes of Sarola Brahmin from Uttarakhand. They are the sole custodians and pandits of the Gangotri temple.

positions.A: The Semwal subcaste's exclusive hereditary right as sole custodians and pandits of the Gangotri temple is a legitimate traditional privilege that should be preserved.
positions.B: The exclusive hereditary control of the Gangotri temple by the Semwal subcaste is an outdated caste-based monopoly that should be opened to broader eligibility.

title: Gudia (caste)
neutral_summary: Gudia or Guria or Gudiya (also known as Madhuvaishya) is a caste found in the Indian states of Odisha and Chhatishgarh, also a small population in Andhra Pradesh. Traditionally their occupation is making of various type of sweets for village ceremonies and festive occasion and subsist on this business. They are also supplier of offerings for village deity. Nowadays they have opened their modern sweet stalls in markets for better business.

positions.A: Gudia should be officially classified as a distinct caste eligible for OBC reservation benefits based on their traditional sweet-making occupation.
positions.B: Gudia should not receive separate caste-based reservation status, as their occupation-based classification does not warrant distinct affirmative action benefits.

title: Kamsali
neutral_summary: Kamsali is a community in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Their traditional profession was as goldsmith. They were part of Vishwakarma group. They are classified as Other Backward Class according to Reservation in the government.

positions.A: Kamsali should retain Other Backward Class status because they remain socially and economically disadvantaged relative to forward castes.
positions.B: Kamsali should not be classified as Other Backward Class because their traditional artisan/goldsmith occupation and Vishwakarma affiliation reflect relatively higher social standing not warranting reservation benefits.

title: Siviyar
neutral_summary: Siviyar (Tamil: சிவியார், lit. 'Chiviyar', also written Chiviar and Tamil: சிவிகையார், lit. 'Chivikaiyar') is a caste found in the Indian state of Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka. They were traditionally palanquin bearers. They are a single community in Sri Lanka, but are however a subcaste of the Idaiyar caste in Tamil Nadu. According to Srinivasa Aiyangar “The Siviyar (palankeen bearers) and the Agattu-Charna sub-division of the Tamil ldaiyan caste are note-worthy, as affording a connecting link between them and the Samantas and Nayars of Malabar.

positions.A: Siviyar constitutes a distinct, independent caste community in its own right, particularly in Sri Lanka.
positions.B: Siviyar is properly classified as a subcaste under the broader Idaiyar caste, as is the case in Tamil Nadu.

title: Gangari Brahmin
neutral_summary: Gangari Brahmin is a Brahmin subcaste originating from the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand, India. They were settled in the villages surrounding the Ganges valley hence known as "Gangari" Brahmins.

positions.A: Gangari Brahmin is a legitimate, distinct Brahmin subcaste with a documented historical origin in the Garhwal region's Ganges valley villages.
positions.B: The classification of Gangari Brahmin as a separate subcaste is a modern or unsubstantiated identity claim rather than a historically distinct group.

title: Gowala (caste)
neutral_summary: Gowala (also spelled as Goala) is a subcaste of Ahir/Yadav community, found in the Indian states of Assam, West Bengal, Tripura and Himachal Pradesh and the neighbouring states of Arunachal Pradesh, Punjab and Chandigarh. Traditionally they are herdsmen or milkmen and considered a prosperous community.

positions.A: Gowala is legitimately a subcaste within the broader Ahir/Yadav community, sharing its traditional pastoral occupation and social identity.
positions.B: Gowala is a distinct caste group in its own right, wrongly subsumed under the Ahir/Yadav umbrella for classification purposes.

title: Dasari (caste)
neutral_summary:
Dasari is a Vaishnava mendicant caste in Telangana region and Andhra Pradesh, India. They are involved in various business, trades, and agriculture. They are part of Gowda (Goud) community.
The history of Dasari caste dates back to centuries.

positions.A: Dasari is a distinct caste in its own right with a unique history and identity separate from the Gowda community.
positions.B: Dasari is properly considered a sub-group within the broader Gowda (Goud) community rather than a fully independent caste.

title: Namadhari
neutral_summary: Namadhari is a term used for people of all castes who follow Sri Vaishnava tradition, sport vermillion nama (a vertical mark) on their foreheads and consider Sri Ramanujacharya as their guru. There are a number of different Namadhari castes like Namadhari Naik in Uttara Kannada, Udupi and Dakshina Kannada Districts, Namdhari Vokkaligas in Malenadu, Namadhari Nagarthas in southern Karnataka and northern Tamil Nadu. and Namadhari Dasari in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Telangana.

positions.A: Namadhari should be recognized as a legitimate umbrella caste identity encompassing distinct communities like Namadhari Naik, Namdhari Vokkaliga, and Namadhari Nagartha, each deserving separate social and administrative recognition.
positions.B: Namadhari is primarily a religious-sectarian marker (denoting Sri Vaishnava tradition and devotion to Ramanujacharya) rather than a genuine independent caste category, and should not be treated as grounds for separate caste-based classification.

title: Malakar
neutral_summary: Malakar (Bengali: মালাকার) is a Bengali Hindu surname spread throughout West Bengal and Bangladesh and also in some parts of Assam, Jharkhand and Tripura. Malakars are traditionally garlanders by trade. They are one of the fourteen castes belonging to 'Nabasakh' group of Bengal.

positions.A: Malakars should be recognized as part of the respectable 'Nabasakh' caste cluster with corresponding ritual and social status within the Bengali Hindu caste hierarchy.
positions.B: The 'Nabasakh' classification and associated caste status of Malakars is a socially constructed label that does not reflect any inherent hierarchical superiority or distinct entitlement.

title: Thimilar
neutral_summary:
Thimilar (Tamil: திமிலர்) is a Sri Lankan Tamil caste found in the northern and eastern coastal areas of Sri Lanka, and globally among the Tamil diaspora. They are traditional artisanal fishers primarily engaged in shallow-water fishing. In Eastern Sri Lanka are they also involved in cattle cultivation.
Historically, they have also been known as Sindhu nāttar (people of Sindh), following their own myth origins.

positions.A: The Thimilar are a distinct Sri Lankan Tamil caste with a unique historical identity traced to Sindh, as reflected in their self-designation as Sindhu nāttar.
positions.B: The Thimilar's claimed Sindhu nāttar origin is a constructed or mythologized identity rather than a verifiable historical lineage.

title: Seerpadar
neutral_summary: Seerpadar (also written as Cirpatar or Seerpadam) is a Tamil caste found in the coastal regions of Eastern Province in Sri Lanka. They are traditionally involved in farming. They are chiefly found in the Veeramunai, Mandur, Thuraineelavanai, Kalmunai,Chenaikudiyiruppu,Kanchikudicharu, Kurumanveli,Naavithanveli,Ezlaam kiraamam,Pathinainthaam kiraamam,Veppaiyadi,Vellaaveli,Paalaiyadiveddai,Muppathainthaam kiraamam,Muppathelaam kiraamam and Periye Kallar regions in the Batticaloa and Ampara District.

positions.A: Seerpadar constitute a distinct Tamil caste group with a specific historical and social identity tied to farming in Sri Lanka's Eastern Province.
positions.B: The caste classification and distinctiveness of Seerpadar as a separate group is a social construct that overstates differences within the broader Tamil farming community.

title: Khar (tribe)
neutral_summary: The Khar (Punjabi: کھر) is a Punjabi Muslim clan of the larger Kharal tribe primarily found in southern Punjab, particularly in the Muzaffargarh District.

positions.A: The Khar are a distinct sub-clan that is genuinely part of the larger Kharal tribe, sharing common ancestry and lineage.
positions.B: The Khar are a separate clan with their own distinct identity and are not legitimately a sub-group of the Kharal tribe.

title: Kurumba Gounder
neutral_summary: Kurumba Gounder is an Indian caste from the state of Tamil Nadu. The Kurumba/Kurumba Gounder community is considered to be a Most Backward Class (MBC) in Tamil Nadu, as they have been historically recognized as socially and financially well settled. They are found in Kongu region - Dindugal, Theni, Namakkal, Trichy and Coimbatore. The Kurumba Gounder community was previously listed as a sub-sect of Kongu Vellalars, but was later moved to the list of Most Backward Classes. A Hindu ceremony characteristic of the Kurumba Gounder are gatherings at a Mahalakshmi temple for a ceremony of supplication for health and success, during which coconuts are smashed on supplicants' heads.

positions.A: Kurumba Gounder is legitimately classified as a Most Backward Class because the community's historical socio-economic status differs meaningfully from that of the broader Kongu Vellalar group.
positions.B: Kurumba Gounder should not be classified separately as a Most Backward Class because the community is historically and socially part of the Kongu Vellalar group, which does not hold MBC status.

title: Singikat
neutral_summary: The Singikat are a Hindu caste found in the state of Haryana, India. They are known as Gyarah.

positions.A: The Singikat should be classified as a distinct caste group with their own social and administrative recognition.
positions.B: The Singikat should be considered part of a broader caste category (Gyarah) rather than a separate distinct group.

title: Shreepali
neutral_summary: The Shreepali Basnet are a clan of the Chhetris originally from the Saipal, Far West Region who got their prominence in Gorkha district of Nepal. They mainly worship 'Masto' as their 'Kulayan' but saipali from Gorkha has changed their worship to "Sishakoti Mahadev", "Veerabhadra", "Mahakali" as their Kul Deuta and Aradhe Devi "Dakshinkali" as Istha deuta in style of Kunwar Rana. They became very powerful during the unification of Nepal and remained so until the emergence of Jung Bahadur Kunwar or later known as Jang Bahadur Rana.

positions.A: The Shreepali Basnet clan's claimed origin from Saipal and their historical prominence during Nepal's unification are accurate and well-documented facts of Chhetri clan history.
positions.B: The Shreepali Basnet clan's claims of ancient origin, unification-era power, and specific religious lineage (worship of Sishakoti Mahadev, Veerabhadra, Mahakali in the style of Kunwar Rana) are unverified or exaggerated genealogical assertions.

title: Duruwa
neutral_summary: The Duruwa, Dhurwa or Dharua is a tribal group found in the Indian states of Chhattisgarh and Odisha. Parji, a Dravidian language, is used by the people in their home domain.

positions.A: The Duruwa, Dhurwa, and Dharua names refer to a single tribal group with shared Dravidian linguistic and cultural identity that should be recognized uniformly for Scheduled Tribe status.
positions.B: The Duruwa, Dhurwa, and Dharua are distinct communities with different regional identities and should be classified and administered separately rather than being merged under one tribal label.

title: Pattanavar
neutral_summary:
Pattanavar (also spelled Pattinavar) is a Tamil caste found in Tamil Nadu, India.
They are a maritime community dominating Chennai, Kanchipuram, Cuddalore, Villuppuram, Thanjavur and Nagapattinam districts of the Coromandel Coast, who have traditionally been involved in fishing, shipment, navy, and trade.

positions.A: Pattanavar should be officially classified and treated as a distinct, unified caste entitled to specific reservation/OBC status based on their traditional maritime occupation.
positions.B: Pattanavar should not be treated as a single homogeneous caste category, as it encompasses distinct sub-groups with different social statuses and claims that do not warrant uniform classification.

title: Daulatana
neutral_summary: Daultana (Urdu: دَولتانہ),  is a clan of Joyia tribe settled in Punjab, Pakistan.

positions.A: The Daulatana clan is a distinct sub-group descended from the Joyia tribe with its own genealogical identity.
positions.B: The Daulatana are not a separate lineage but simply a branch fully subsumed within the broader Joyia tribal identity.

title: Piramalai Kallar
neutral_summary: Piramalai Kallars is a sub-caste of the Kallars and thus are part of the Mukkulathor community that also includes the Maravar and Agamudayar castes. They belong to Other Backward class/Denotified class in Tamil Nadu.

positions.A: The Piramalai Kallars' historical classification as a 'criminal tribe' under British colonial law was an unjust and discriminatory label that continues to stigmatize the community today.
positions.B: The Piramalai Kallars' current designation as a Denotified/Backward Class reflects legitimate historical socio-economic disadvantage and warrants continued affirmative action protections, not colonial-era stigma.

title: Pathani
neutral_summary:
The Paatni (Kumaoni: पाटनी) are an ethnic Kumaoni Rajput group of the Attigoan and Kamsyar region of Gangolihat tehsil Pithoragarh district of the Kumaon Himalayas of the Indian state of Uttarakhand.
Paatni people are members of a Chandravanshi Kshatriya clan that migrated from the town of Patan in Rajasthan to their current location in Uttarakhand in the early 16th century. Atkinson described them as the groups holding small principalities in Kumaon at the end of Katyuri rule and the advent of the Chand dynasty in Kumaon. After a brief stint with the Chands, they were awarded a grant of the Patti of Attigaon and Kamsyar i.e. the area from Ganaigangoli to Banspatan.

positions.A: The Paatni are a genuine Chandravanshi Kshatriya Rajput clan descended from migrants from Patan, Rajasthan, who held historical principalities in Kumaon.
positions.B: The claimed Rajput/Kshatriya origin and Rajasthani migration narrative of the Paatni is a constructed or embellished genealogy rather than a verified historical fact.

title: Tarkhan (Punjab)
neutral_summary:
The Tarkhan is a caste found in the Punjab region of India and Pakistan. They are traditionally carpenters by occupation.
The Hindu members of this clan are generally identified as Khatis, Suthars or Lohars following the Vishwakarma community of India. Tarkhan Sikhs are among those groups who are identified as Ramgarhias, after the Misl leader Jassa Singh Ramgarhia. Despite Sikhism generally rejecting the caste system, it does have its own very similar socio-economic hierarchy and in that the Ramgarhias, of which the Tarkhans are a part, rank second only to the Jat Sikhs, thanks to significant economic and social power that elevated this middle class group from its lower caste confines.
According to the 1921 census of India, which may not be reliable, some Tarkhan Sikhs owned large areas of land and, in some cases, whole villages.
In 2001, the Punjab Government included Ramgarhia, Tarkhan and Dhiman in the list of Other Backward Classes (OBC) to improve their economic conditions. They were also added in the list of backward classes by the governments of Haryana and Himachal Pradesh.

positions.A: The Tarkhan/Ramgarhia community's inclusion in the Other Backward Classes list is justified because they historically faced caste-based social exclusion despite some economic gains.
positions.B: The Tarkhan/Ramgarhia community's inclusion in the Other Backward Classes list is unjustified because their significant economic and social power, including land ownership, means they do not warrant backward class benefits.

title: Turpu Kapu
neutral_summary:
Turpu Kapu is an eastern area name of the Kapu caste is an Indian caste in the state of Andhra Pradesh. This caste belongs to the Other Backward Class (OBC) category added by the Government of Andhra Pradesh .  They are primarily found in the erstwhile districts of Srikakulam, Vizianagaram and Visakhapatnam with smaller numbers in other regions of the state. Traditionally they were warriors and farmers. They are a politically prominent community in the Uttarandhra region of the state.
The word 'Turpu' means eastern in Telugu, an appellation based on their preponderance in the northeastern region of Andhra (Uttarandhra).

positions.A: Turpu Kapu's inclusion in the Other Backward Class (OBC) category is justified given their socio-economic status and historical marginalization relative to dominant castes.
positions.B: Turpu Kapu's inclusion in the OBC category is an unjustified political concession that dilutes reservation benefits meant for more disadvantaged communities.

title: Sadar Lingayats
neutral_summary: Sadar Lingayats (ಸಾದರ ಲಿಂಗಾಯತ) is a sub-caste of Lingayats, the community that inhabit Central Karnataka region of the Karnataka state in India. The community, also called as ʼʼSadaruʼʼ or ʼʼSadaru Okkaligasʼʼ, is a cultivating caste and were once acted as a native militia and were into trading of grains. The  land-owning feudal community vows its allegiance to Taralabalu Jagadguru Brihanmath, Sirigere.  It is one of the dominant sub-castes of the Lingayat community. They are politically strong and among the richest sects in Lingayatism. However, historical and colonial records suggest that they were originally adherents of Jainism. The community uses honorific surname Gowda or Gauda. Desai, Patel, Patil and Bommai are some of the prominent surnames used by the community. They are mostly found in Davangere, Vijayanagara, Haveri, Chitradurga, Shivamogga, Ballari, Bagalkot, and Hubbali-Dharwad districts of Karnataka. They were considered as one of the component caste or an ethnic group under the Vokkaliga Community, as per the Mysore Gazetteer.

positions.A: Sadar Lingayats are historically and religiously rooted Lingayats whose identity and social status derive from allegiance to the Taralabalu Jagadguru Brihanmath and Lingayat tradition.
positions.B: Historical and colonial records indicate that Sadar Lingayats were originally Jain adherents later absorbed into the Lingayat and Vokkaliga social framework, making their Lingayat identity a later reclassification rather than an original one.

title: Paika (community)
neutral_summary: The Paik or Paika (Odia:ପାଇକ) is a Militia community, found in Odisha state of India.

positions.A: The Paika constitute a distinct historical community with a unique martial identity deserving separate social and political recognition, including reservation benefits.
positions.B: The Paika are merely an occupational militia group defined by former military service rather than a distinct caste or ethnic community warranting separate recognition.

title: Ilai Vaniyar
neutral_summary: Ilia Vaniyar is a Tamil-speaking caste mainly from south Tamil Nadu. Other names they are referred are Senaiyar, Senaithalaivar, Moopanar(In Tirunelveli District) Mudaliar, Pillai. They belong to the Vaishya varna.

positions.A: Ilai Vaniyar community rightfully belongs to the Vaishya varna, reflecting their traditional social and economic status.
positions.B: The claim that Ilai Vaniyar belongs to the Vaishya varna is a self-ascribed status not universally recognized within the traditional caste hierarchy.

title: Kurukkal
neutral_summary:
The Kurukkal, also known as Gurukkal are an Ambalavasi caste of Tamil origin. Originally a patrilineal community found in Travancore and Malabar region of present-day Kerala, whose traditional function was that of temple servants, they became matrilineal towards the end of the 18th century under the influence of Nair caste. Their rank lies below the Nambudhiri, Varma, Pillai, Sacred thread wearing Ambalavasi castes of Travancore and Malabar. Kurukkal women had hypergamous marriages with higher caste men of Travancore and Kurukkal men struck similar relationships with women from the matrilineal Maran caste.

The community's position in the Hindu ritual ranking system known as varna is disputed. In Kerala, they generally claim to be Tamil Iyer Brahmins and Ambalavasi caste.

positions.A: The Kurukkal community should be recognized as Tamil Iyer Brahmins, placing them within the Brahmin varna category.
positions.B: The Kurukkal community should be classified as an Ambalavasi caste, ranking below Brahmin and other higher Ambalavasi groups rather than as true Brahmins.

title: Raut (caste)
neutral_summary:
Raut (also spelled as Rout) is an Indian caste, whose traditional occupation is to rule.
The  Rauts are mainly found in the Chhattisgarh state, and the neighbouring states of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.  Traditionally, they were predominantly distributed in the districts of Durg, Raipur, Bastar, Nagpur and Bhandara.

positions.A: The Raut caste's traditional occupation and status as rulers reflect a historically legitimate claim to a distinct social position within the caste hierarchy.
positions.B: Claims about the Raut caste's traditional ruling occupation are exaggerated social narratives that do not correspond to any verifiable historical political authority.

title: Rautia
neutral_summary:
During the British Colonial some populations of Rautia caste migrate from their native state to Assam, Bengal and Nepal for searching job in tea gardens and became the natives of these states.
The Rautia/Routia is a Hindu Caste community and Kshatriya Varna by its origin. The Rautia Caste is a upper caste in its Sadan ethnic community and because of being a Sadan caste, the mother tongue culture is Sadani which is known as Nagpuri or Sadri found in the states of Jharkhand, Bihar, Chhattisgarh Odisha, Assam  and Bengal in India. The presence of Rautia caste is also seen in countries like Nepal and Bangladesh.

positions.A: The Rautia caste is a Kshatriya-origin upper caste within the Sadan ethnic community, with a distinct historical and cultural identity tied to Sadani/Nagpuri/Sadri language and traditions.
positions.B: The Rautia caste's claimed Kshatriya and upper-caste status within the Sadan community is a contested or self-asserted identity rather than an universally recognized historical classification.

title: Nador (caste)
neutral_summary: Nador (ನಾಡೋರ) or Nadavaru (Kannada: ನಾಡವರು) or Nadavar (ನಾಡವರ) is the name of a caste from Karnataka, India. Members of the castle are found primarily in the coastal areas of Uttara Kannada district, formerly known as North Canara, with many members also spread throughout the world. Caste members traditionally speak the Nadavar dialect of Kannada called Nadavar Kannada (ನಾಡವರ ಕನ್ನಡ). They are a prominent agriculture community of the Uttara Kannada district of Karnataka, India.

positions.A: Nadavaru/Nador should be recognized as a distinct agricultural caste of Uttara Kannada with its own historical and linguistic identity separate from other Kannada-speaking communities.
positions.B: Nadavaru/Nador is better understood as a subgroup or offshoot of a broader regional caste cluster rather than a wholly distinct, independent caste category.

title: Kathia
neutral_summary: The Kathia is a Muslim tribe of Pakistani Punjab. Many leaders of Kathia tribe were main participants in the Indian Rebellion of 1857 led by Rai Ahmad Khan Kharal.

positions.A: The Kathia tribe played a central and heroic role in the Indian Rebellion of 1857 under Rai Ahmad Khan Kharal, reflecting its historical prominence in Punjab's resistance movements.
positions.B: The role of the Kathia tribe in the 1857 rebellion is often exaggerated in tribal histories and folklore, overstating its actual historical significance compared to other participants.

title: Nagartha
neutral_summary:
The Nagartha or Nagarta are Vaishya as per Hindu caste of south India of merchants or agriculturalists.
The Nagartha caste contains two main divisions, Vaishnavas or Namadhari Nagarthas and Shiv  or Lingadhari Nagarthas.

positions.A: The Nagartha community rightfully holds Vaishya status within the Hindu caste system as merchants or agriculturalists of south India.
positions.B: The Vaishya classification claimed by the Nagartha community is a disputed or self-asserted status rather than a universally recognized caste ranking.

title: Dikshitar
neutral_summary:
Dīkṣitars  or Thillai Vazh Anthaanar are a Vedic Shaiva Brahmin servitor community of Tamil Nadu, India, who are based mainly in the town of Chidambaram. Smartha (especially the Vadamas), Sri Vaishnava and other Brahmins in South India also carry the surname Dikshitars, but are different from the Chidambaram Dikshitar.
They are an exclusive group of Brahmins learned in the Vedas and yagnas (sacrifices) who also serve as the hereditary trustees of the Nataraja temple in Chidambaram. They are also called Thillai Muvayiravar or the Three Thousand of Thillai. Every Dikshitar once he is married becomes as of right a trustee and archaka of the Nataraja temple. A practice unique to the community is that the priests wear the tuft of hair in front of the head similar to the Nambuthiri Brahmans of Kerala.

positions.A: The Dikshitar community's hereditary right to exclusively administer and serve as trustees of the Nataraja temple should be preserved as a traditional religious practice.
positions.B: The temple's administration should be subject to government or judicial oversight rather than remaining an exclusive hereditary privilege of the Dikshitar caste.

key_entities: Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department

title: Karmali tribe
neutral_summary: The Karmali is an artisan tribe of Jharkhand. It is composed of blacksmiths. They are mainly concentrated in Ramgarh, Bokaro, Hazaribagh, Giridih and Ranchi district of Jharkhand and sizable populations are also found in Aurangabad, Rohtas of Bihar; West Bengal and Assam. They speak Khotta language at home and Hindi language with society. As per 1981 census their population in the state was 38,651. They are considered as Scheduled Tribe in West Bengal and Jharkhand.

positions.A: The Karmali qualify as a genuine Scheduled Tribe due to their distinct artisanal (blacksmith) identity, language, and historical socio-economic marginalization, justifying their reserved status in Jharkhand and West Bengal.
positions.B: The Karmali are more accurately an occupational caste group rather than a tribe, and their Scheduled Tribe classification may be a political or administrative decision that does not reflect genuine tribal characteristics.

title: 24 Manai Telugu Chettiars
neutral_summary: The 24 Manai Telugu Chettiar (24MTC) also called as Telugu Chetty is a community who are predominantly found in the states of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala, Telangana in India, as well as Sri Lanka.

positions.A: The 24 Manai Telugu Chettiar community claims a distinct historical and social identity rooted in Telugu merchant traditions that warrants specific caste recognition and status.
positions.B: Critics and some caste classification bodies argue that the community's claimed status and origin narrative are exaggerated or contested, and that it should be classified alongside other similar trading castes without special distinction.

title: Kandu
neutral_summary:
'Kanu'  or Kandu is a Baniya or Vaishya caste that has been historically associated with trading activities-- sweet-making, shop-keeping, trading etc. in India and Nepal.  One of their notable business activities is confectionery.
They have been associated with the states Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Purvanchal area of Uttar pradesh and Nepal (Madhesi region) 
Like many other Bania communities, they are undergoing urbanisation. Many rural Kanu’s are shopkeepers and trader. They have a state wise caste association, the Kanu Vaishya Mahasabha, which act as a both as an instrument of social control as well as communal welfare association.

positions.A: The Kandu (Kanu) community rightfully belongs to the Baniya/Vaishya caste category based on their traditional trading and business occupations.
positions.B: The Kandu (Kanu) community's claim to Vaishya/Baniya status is disputed and they should instead be classified under a different caste category, such as Other Backward Class, for reservation and social purposes.

title: Langrial clan
neutral_summary: The Langrial  (لنگريال)  is a clan of Jats in Pakistan. Some Langrials claim Rajput descent. They are scattered across the Punjab and some parts of  KPK.

positions.A: The Langrial clan is fundamentally of Jat origin, with any Rajput claims being later social assertions rather than genealogical fact.
positions.B: Some Langrials are legitimately of Rajput descent, and the clan's classification as purely Jat overlooks this distinct lineage.

title: Hebbar Iyengar
neutral_summary: Hebbar Iyengar or Hebbari Srivaishnava  is a caste of Hindu Brahmins of Tamil and Kannada origin whose members follow the Visishtadvaita philosophy propounded by Ramanuja. They are found primarily in the Indian state of Karnataka especially in the southern districts. They speak Hebbar Tamil, a minority dialect of Tamil, reflecting extensive contact with Kannada.

positions.A: Hebbar Iyengars originated as a Tamil Brahmin community that migrated to Karnataka and later adopted local linguistic influences.
positions.B: Hebbar Iyengars are a distinct Kannada-origin Brahmin community whose identity is not simply an extension of Tamil Iyengar migration.

title: Kudumbi
neutral_summary: The Kudumbi, also referred to as the Kunubis, the Kurumbi, or the Kunbi (Konkani: [kuɽumbiː, kunubiː]), are traditionally a Konkani-speaking farming community residing in Kerala, India.

positions.A: The Kudumbi community was historically subjected to servitude and displacement by upper-caste Goud Saraswat Brahmin migrants fleeing Goa, and this history justifies their claim to Scheduled Caste/Tribe status and affirmative action benefits.
positions.B: The Kudumbi community's origins and social status do not warrant special reservation classification, as their historical position as a farming caste does not meet the criteria applied to officially recognized Scheduled Castes or Tribes.

title: Bangial
neutral_summary: Bangial is a Punjabi Rajput Muslim tribe of Panwar Rajputs, found principally in the Pothohar region of Punjab, Pakistan. They are named after their ancestor Raja Bangash Khan, whose forefathers migrated from Dhara Nagri (now Dhar, India). They are also present in Gujrat, Darya Khan Tehsil, Jhelum, Azad Jammu & Kashmir and Gujranwala districts in Punjab.

positions.A: The Bangial tribe are genuine Panwar Rajputs descended from Raja Bangash Khan, tracing lineage back to Dhara Nagri.
positions.B: The claimed Rajput ancestry and lineage of the Bangial tribe is a constructed or unverifiable genealogical tradition rather than a proven historical fact.

title: Bhavsar
neutral_summary:
Bhavsar or "Bhavsara Kshatriya" is a Hindu caste. As time passed, the Bhavsar community was made up of community involved in Calico printing business. In Gujarat, Bhavsar are also known as Baniya (Vaniya) as the Bhavsar community has a long history of trading in textile, agriculture and other retail businesses. Subcategories in Bhavsar community are Hindu Bhavsar and Jain Bhavsar which represents diverse religions practices within Bhavsar community.
In the early 1850s, Bhavsars earned their riches through the clothing business, farmlands, havelis, and horses, but most Bhavsars are now pursuing modern-day occupations, including private sector or public sector jobs. After the Independence of India, Bhavsars did not get much in the way of government grants or opportunities. Bhavsars are being considered in open category. With limited alternatives (including Government grants, or benefits, after independence) Bhavsar youth mainly went towards higher education categories including engineering, medical, business degree and others.
Surnames of Marathi-speaking Bhavsar people include Anchalkar, Gondkar, Achekar, and Vaijwade, among others.

positions.A: Bhavsars are correctly classified in the open category since they historically attained economic prosperity through trade and business, making them ineligible for caste-based reservation benefits.
positions.B: Bhavsars have been unfairly denied government grants, quotas, and reservation benefits after independence despite facing socio-economic disadvantages comparable to other backward castes.

title: Kadava Patidar
neutral_summary:
The Kadava Patidar (also variously spelled Kadwa, Kadva) are a sub-caste of the Patidar caste in India's state of Gujarat. They are mainly found in North Gujarat and Ahmedabad. 
The name "Kadava" comes from "Kadi", a former district that existed during the Baroda State. In one origin myth, the goddess Umā created 52 statues from clay and her husband, Shiva, breathed life into them. These 52 people became the founders of the 52 sections among the Kadvas.
The Kadava Patidar are primarily engaged in agriculture, with many members of the community being farmers and landowners. They are known for their strong sense of community and adherence to traditional values and customs. The Kadava Patidar have a well-organized community structure, with various organizations and institutions working towards the welfare and development of the community. Historically, the Kadava Patidar have been involved in various social and political movements in Gujarat. They played a significant role in the Indian independence movement, with many members of the community actively participating in the struggle against British colonial rule. In the post-independence era, the Kadava Patidar have continued to be politically active, with several members of the community holding important positions in the state government and local administration.
The Kadvas used to have a unique marriage custom in which marriages were only conducted once every ten years. This led to girls being married at a very young age lest they be too old the next time a marriage year came. These young girls would be married to a flower ball which was then thrown in the well, and when the girls reached proper marriable age they could conduct their second marriage at any time. The 1868 (Samvat 1925) caste constitution first allowed annual marriages to be conducted. This marriage custom was noted to be in decline by 1911. In 1922, the Kadva Seva Mandal organized a caste conference which abolished the deccenial marriage custom.

positions.A: The Kadva decennial marriage custom, which married young girls to flower balls to avoid them 'aging out' of marriage eligibility, was a harmful patriarchal practice akin to child marriage that required correction.
positions.B: The Kadva marriage custom was a functional cultural adaptation to the rarity of marriage years, and the community itself reformed it through internal caste conferences without needing outside intervention.

title: Godha
neutral_summary: The Godha are Jain tribal caste people found in the state of Gujarat in India having roots in Rajasthan. They are also known as Gondha and Gonda. The Godha sometimes (depending on region) use Dengar as a community surname.

positions.A: The Godha should be officially classified as a Scheduled Tribe, reflecting their tribal origins and cultural distinctiveness rooted in Rajasthan.
positions.B: The Godha should not receive Scheduled Tribe status, as their identity is primarily a religious (Jain) caste grouping rather than a distinct tribal community.

title: Rajdhoves
neutral_summary: Rajdhob or Rajdhov is an indigenous group of people based mainly in Terai of Nepal. In general, they are categorized as Madhesi.

positions.A: Rajdhobs should be formally recognized and classified as part of the Madhesi community with corresponding political and social rights.
positions.B: Rajdhobs constitute a distinct indigenous group whose identity should not be subsumed under the broader Madhesi classification.

title: Barujibi
neutral_summary:
Barujibi (Bengali: বারুজীবী/বারুজীবি) or Barui (Bengali: বারুই) is a Bengali Hindu agrarian caste found in India and Bangladesh. Their traditional occupation is cultivation of Betel. Barujibi is one of the fourteen castes belonging to 'Nabasakh' group of Bengal.
They are listed as Other Backward Class in West Bengal as "Barujibi, Barui" and in the Central List as recommended by Mandal Commission. Although socio-culturally different, this caste is akin in terms of occupation to Barai, Tamboli and Chaurasia caste groups of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, Tammali in Andhra Pradesh, Bariji in Odisha, Barjubi in Assam.

positions.A: Barujibi/Barui caste members face genuine social and educational disadvantages that justify their classification as Other Backward Class and inclusion in reservation policies.
positions.B: The inclusion of Barujibi/Barui as Other Backward Class is an unwarranted extension of caste-based reservation that does not reflect their actual socio-economic status.

title: Hatwal
neutral_summary: Hatwal is one of the 36 sub-castes of Sarola Brahmins and their toponymic surname from Hat, a village in the Chamoli district of Uttarakhand, India.

positions.A: Hatwal is a legitimate toponymic sub-caste surname derived from the village of Hat, reflecting genuine Sarola Brahmin lineage and heritage.
positions.B: Caste-based sub-classifications like Hatwal are social constructs without objective basis and merely perpetuate caste distinctions.

title: Gandhabanik
neutral_summary:
Gandhabanik (Bengali: গন্ধবণিক) is a Bengali Hindu trading caste, who as the caste name suggests, traditionally used to trade in perfumes, cosmetics, spices etc. They were also  engaged in agriculture. As of late nineteenth century they were one of the fourteen castes belonging to Nabasakh group.
It is believed that the legendary sea merchant Chand Sadagar of ancient Champaknagar was from Gandhabanik community.

positions.A: Gandhabanik should be recognized as a high-status Vaishya (mercantile) caste with ancient lineage tracing back to legendary figures like Chand Sadagar.
positions.B: Gandhabanik's claims to elevated Vaishya/Kshatriya status are later social assertions rather than reflecting their historical position within the Nabasakh group of trading castes.

title: Mal (caste)
neutral_summary:
The Mal is a Hindu caste found in the state of West Bengal and Jharkhand.
Mal and Malla are derived from the Sanskrit word malla, meaning wrestler.
Paharia Mal or Mal Paharia is considered as Scheduled Tribe while the other Mal groups are considered as Scheduled Castes by the Government of West Bengal.

positions.A: Mal Paharia should retain Scheduled Tribe status while other Mal groups are classified as Scheduled Castes, reflecting distinct socio-historical origins.
positions.B: All Mal groups, including Mal Paharia, should be classified under a single uniform category since they share a common caste origin and name.

title: Koli Christians
neutral_summary: Koli Christians are Koli people who profess Christianity in India, they are part of the Koli caste of Bombay East Indians, who are the indigenous ethnic people of the Seven Islands of Bombay, the Bombay metropolitan area & the northern Konkan region; in which lies the city of Mumbai (Bombay). The Koli Christians continue to hold on to some of their Koli customs/ values as the part of Koli caste, in spite of their conversions from Brahmanism to Christianity & in the former Bom Bahia of Portuguese India. Christian Kolis are also known as Thankar & Gaonkar Kolis; they played an important role in building churches & convents in the northern Konkan division of present-day Maharashtra.

positions.A: Koli Christians retain a distinct indigenous Koli ethnic and caste identity, preserving Koli customs and social status despite their conversion to Christianity.
positions.B: Conversion to Christianity fundamentally redefines Koli converts as members of a new religious community, superseding their prior caste-based Koli identity and customs.

title: Mukkuvar (India)
neutral_summary: The Mukkuvar are a maritime ethnic group found in the Indian states of Kerala, Tamil Nadu and the Eastern and North Western coastal regions of Sri Lanka. They are mostly found on the Malabar Coast,  and Kanyakumari district, Tamil Nadu, who have traditionally been involved in fishing and other maritime activities.

positions.A: The Mukkuvar community should be classified and recognized as a Backward Class/Other Backward Class (OBC) entitled to corresponding reservations and social status.
positions.B: The Mukkuvar community's traditional caste status has been misrepresented or inflated, and they do not warrant the backward-class classification and associated reservation benefits some claim.

title: Rajakulathor (caste)
neutral_summary: The Rajakula people, who are also collectively known as Rajaka, are native to the Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, India. They comprise the Vannar, Madivala and Agasa social groups that share a common myth of origin and claim to have once been members of various ancient South Indian dynasties.

positions.A: The Rajakula people are legitimately descended from ancient South Indian dynasties, and their claimed royal origin myth reflects a genuine historical lineage.
positions.B: The Rajakula people's claim of descent from ancient royal dynasties is a status-elevating origin myth rather than an accurate historical account, and they are more accurately classified as a traditional washermen (Vannar/Madivala/Agasa) caste grouping.

title: Puran (caste)
neutral_summary: Puran (Bhanja Puran or Tamudia Puran) is a caste group of East India. They are primarily inhabitants of the states of Odisha, West Bengal and Jharkhand. They are currently considered a Other Backward Class, but Jharkhand and Odisha government proposed to include them in the Scheduled Tribes list. They speak Puran Bhasa, which is a blend of Tamaria and Odia language. As per 2011 census the language recorded 12,375 speaker in India.

positions.A: The Puran community should be reclassified from Other Backward Class to Scheduled Tribe status, as proposed by the Jharkhand and Odisha governments, in recognition of their distinct tribal identity and needs.
positions.B: The Puran community should remain classified as Other Backward Class rather than being granted Scheduled Tribe status, since reclassification could be seen as unwarranted or disruptive to existing quota allocations.

title: Chunaru
neutral_summary:
Chunaru (Bengali: চুনারু) or Chunari is a Bengali Hindu caste whose traditional occupation is the manufacture of slaked lime from the shell of snails. After the advent of quick lime from limestone and the arrival of cement as mortar ingredient, the Chunaru struggled to make a living of their traditional vocation and gradually dwindled in numbers.
According to Maniklal Sinha, there are only about 200 to 300 Chunaru families in West Bengal today.

positions.A: Traditional occupational castes like the Chunaru deserve continued official recognition and support to preserve their cultural heritage and livelihood.
positions.B: Caste-based occupational classifications like Chunaru are outdated and should not be perpetuated through official recognition in modern society.

title: Maulika Kayastha
neutral_summary: Maulika Kayastha is a sub-caste of Bengali Kayasthas originated from the Bengal region of Indian subcontinent. The Bengali Kayasthas are subdivided into different classes or ranks and also divided in terms of their geographical locations.  According to legend, the Bengali Hindu King Ballal Sen started the ranking system of Brahmins, Kayasthas and Baidyas in Bengal. The highest ranked Brahmins and Kayasthas are known as Kulin Brahmins and Kulin Kayasthas, respectively, and those Kayasthas not considered to be Kulins are designated Maulikas, Mauliks, Mouliks or Moulikas.

positions.A: The traditional Kulin-Maulika ranking system reflects a legitimate historical social hierarchy among Bengali Kayasthas established by King Ballal Sen.
positions.B: The Kulin-Maulika ranking system is an artificial and discriminatory social stratification that unfairly subordinates Maulika Kayasthas within their own caste.

title: Koviyar
neutral_summary: Koviyar (Tamil: கோவியர், romanized: Kōviyar, also known as Covia) is a Tamil caste found in Sri Lanka. They are traditional agriculturalists, temple guardians and temple workers but also included feudal lords, warriors, mercenaries, merchants, landowners and temple patrons.Kattavarayan as caste deity is observed by the Koviar. They are reputed as a ritually dominant caste and regarded as the "cousin" caste of the more numerical dominant caste, Sri Lankan Vellalar.

positions.A: Koviyar is a ritually and socially high-ranking caste, closely allied to and considered a 'cousin' of the dominant Vellalar caste, with a history of feudal lords, warriors, and landowners.
positions.B: Koviyar's status has historically been subordinate to the Vellalar caste, with its members primarily serving as agricultural laborers and temple servants rather than holding genuine parity in social rank.

title: Samvedi
neutral_summary: Samvedis or Samvedi Brahmins are an Indian Hindu Brahmin community, originating from a group of classical musicians and classical dancers. They follow Sama Veda and believed to have been originated from Odisha, India.

positions.A: Samvedis are a legitimate Brahmin community whose ancestors were classical musicians and dancers originating from Odisha who followed the Sama Veda.
positions.B: Samvedis' claim to Brahmin status and their Odisha origin narrative is a constructed or contested identity rather than a firmly established historical fact.

title: Shaikhzada
neutral_summary: Shaikhzadah or Shaikhzada (Urdu: شيخ زاده) is a Baloch tribe in Balochistan, Pakistan.

positions.A: The Shaikhzada are a distinct Baloch tribe with their own separate lineage and identity within Balochistan.
positions.B: The Shaikhzada are better understood as a sub-group or offshoot connected to broader Baloch or Sheikh lineage classifications rather than a fully independent tribe.

title: Qidwai
neutral_summary:
The Qidwai or Kidwai (Urdu: قدوائی, Arabic: قدوائی) are a community of Muslim Sheikhs in South Asia, who migrated from present day Israel and Palestine. They belong to the  Israelites tribe of the regions. Their lineage which traces back to Isaac, is different to the rest of the Muslims whose lineage comes from the other son of Abraham, Ishmael. Due to the fact, that their lineage is from actual wife of Abraham (Sarah) and not through (Hagar), Kidwais were always monotheist, unlike rest of the Arabs. They are mostly now settled in the state of Uttar Pradesh in India and Karachi, Sindh, Pakistan. They are also settled in areas of the Middle East specifically, Saudi Arabia, Palestine and Qatar. 
The Qidwai, together with the Khan, Milki, Malik and Chaudhary form a community of substantial landowners.

positions.A: The Qidwai/Kidwai community has a genuine Israelite lineage tracing back to Isaac, distinguishing them from other Muslim groups descended from Ishmael.
positions.B: The claimed Israelite/Isaac lineage of the Qidwai/Kidwai is an unsubstantiated genealogical narrative rather than a verified historical fact.

title: Tadvi Bhil
neutral_summary: The Tadvi Bhil is a tribal community found in the states of Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan in India. They are a clan of the larger Bhil ethnic group. They use the surname Tadvi or sometimes the name of their Kul or Gan; the Dhankas of Gujarat and Maharashtra use Tadvi or Tetariya.

positions.A: Tadvi Bhil should be recognized as a distinct Scheduled Tribe entitled to its own reservation and welfare benefits separate from related groups like the Dhanka.
positions.B: Tadvi Bhil should be classified together with related groups such as the Dhanka under a shared tribal category, since they share surnames and origins.

title: Max Bodenheimer
neutral_summary: Max Isidor Bodenheimer (Hebrew: מקס בודנהיימר; 12 March 1865 – 19 July 1940) was a lawyer and one of the main figures in German Zionism. An associate of Theodor Herzl, he was the first president of the Zionist Federation of Germany and one of the founders of the Jewish National Fund. After his flight in 1933 from Nazi Germany, and a short sojourn in Holland, he settled in Palestine in 1935.

positions.A: Zionism, as advanced by figures like Bodenheimer, was a legitimate national liberation movement seeking self-determination for the Jewish people in their ancestral homeland.
positions.B: Zionism, as advanced by figures like Bodenheimer, was a colonial-nationalist project that disregarded the rights of the indigenous Arab population of Palestine.

title: Cheema (person)
neutral_summary:
Cheema (also spelled Chima) is a Punjabi Jat clan and surname in Pakistan and India. 
Cheemas were historically recorded among the tribes of the Rachna Doab.

positions.A: Cheema is fundamentally a Punjabi Jat clan, and its historical identity should be classified within the Jat tribal framework.
positions.B: Cheema is a broader surname/clan identity that extends beyond Jat classification and should not be narrowly tied to Jat ethnic categorization.

title: Goud
neutral_summary: Goud is a caste, predominantly settled in the Indian states of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. The Gouds have been traditionally involved in the occupation of toddy tapping. They are a rapidly developing community in both economical and political realms in Telangana.

positions.A: The Goud community deserves stronger reservation benefits and OBC/ST classification recognition due to their historical socio-economic backwardness tied to toddy tapping occupation.
positions.B: The Goud community's current classification and reservation status is adequate and should not be expanded, as doing so risks unfairly diverting benefits from more disadvantaged groups.

title: Shunri
